Chapter One: Early Life and the Making of an Outsider.
Have you ever felt that itch—that quiet restlessness, deep inside, nudging you to push past the boundaries everyone else seems happy to accept? For some folks, it’s just a passing thought. But for others, it shapes everything they become.
In the early 1900s, in Baltimore, Maryland, a young woman was growing up in a family that cared a lot about tradition and social standing. From the outside, her life looked pretty comfortable. But even as a kid, she could sense she was meant for something more—something that didn’t fit neatly into the world her parents imagined for her.
Picture it: her father was a successful banker, her mother cared deeply about fitting in. Their expectations were clear—finishing school, polite society, a good marriage. But she dreamed of adventure. She loved horses, the outdoors, that feeling of pushing past her own limits. You could just tell—this wasn’t someone who’d be content sitting quietly at the edge of the room.
As she got older, those dreams only grew. She wanted to travel, to see the world, to make a real difference. The problem? The world she lived in wasn’t exactly built for women with big ambitions. Doors to diplomacy, politics, and adventure were mostly closed—especially for women who didn’t fit the mold. But she didn’t let that stop her. Instead, she kept looking for a way in.
Then, everything changed in her early twenties. It happened so suddenly—a hunting trip, a misstep, and a shotgun accident left her with a terrible injury. After several failed surgeries, doctors had to amputate her left leg below the knee. For most people, that would’ve been the end of any adventurous dreams. But not for her.
She learned to walk with a wooden prosthetic, which she later named “Cuthbert.” Every step hurt, but her determination never wavered. She forced herself to adapt, to keep moving forward—even when the pain was constant.
Over the next few years, she kept searching for her place in the world. She studied in Europe, picked up new languages, and even tried to join the U.S. Foreign Service. But time after time, she ran into barriers—her gender, her disability, and all those unwritten rules about what women were allowed to do. The State Department made it clear: a woman with a wooden leg didn’t fit their idea of a diplomat. Each rejection stung, but she refused to let it define her. If anything, it made her more determined.
Most people, faced with that kind of resistance, might have given up. But for her, every setback was just another lesson. She learned to move quietly, to observe, to adapt. She became skilled at blending in, at hiding her pain, at using her outsider status to her advantage. Being on the margins gave her a perspective others just didn’t have. The world’s indifference hardened into her armor, and her difference became her greatest strength.
By the late 1930s, as Europe inched closer to war, she found herself in Paris, working in a minor diplomatic post. The city was buzzing with tension—everything felt uncertain, on the edge of something big. And for someone who’d always felt a bit out of place, the chaos felt oddly familiar. She was ready for whatever came next, even if she couldn’t quite see what that would be.
